newsitem.title: USA: U.S. banks not expected to be hurt by card curbs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. banks not expected to be hurt by card curbs.

text.p: Although a Federal Reserve survey confirmed Monday some well-publicized trends about rising credit card losses, analysts said profits of U.S. banks were not likely to suffer very much.
The survey said banks have been tightening standards for consumer loans and putting stricter limits on credit cards. A rise ln bankruptcies was cited as a factor.
"The thing to keep in mind is that the typical bank makes seven percent of its loans in cards," said Anthony Davis, an analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds.
"The earnings contribution from that line of business (credit cards) is typically in the range of five pecent of profits," Davis said.
He said the card business in fact was still one of the most profitable segments of the industry. But with tighter standards it will be less profitable than before.

George Salem, an analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison, said the tighter standards would reduce loss rates in a year or two while cutting revenues immediately. "It's paying the piper for something you should have done a lot sooner," he said. He added that the Fed survey contained nothing new.

An article in the New York Times on Sunday said if present trends continue, a record 1.1 million Americans would file for personal bankruptcy this year. The old record was 900,000 filings in 1992. High levels of bankruptcies in the past have been associated with recession, while the U.S economy is currently in an expansionary phase.

Carl Campbell, president and chief executive of Keystone Financial Inc, told Reuters in an interview Monday that an unusual twist in the current wave was that many borrowers who had not necessarily been delinquent in their payments filed for bankruptcy rather suddenly.

Campbell, who heads a Harrisburg, Pa-based bank holding company with $5 billion in assets, said the bankrupticies often follow some "triggering event" such as a wage-earner in a two-income family losing a job, a divorce or illness.
"Bankruptcy doesn't have the stigma that it once did," Campbell said, adding that from his "old-fashioned and conservative" point of view it is not a healthy trend.
The banker said the underlying trends in delinquencies must be watched carefully, though the situation overall is "not a real panicky trend."
